units.title: Even and odd numbers
units.description: Recognise even and odd numbers by pairing objects and looking at the last digit.
learningObjectives: Pair objects to decide whether a count is even or odd
Use the last digit to classify large numbers

blocks.text: Every whole number is either **even** or **odd**. A number is even if its objects can be arranged in pairs with nothing left over, and odd if one object is always left without a partner.
This idea of pairing is called the **parity** of a number. Parity asks only one question: *does it pair up completely, or is there one left over?*

blocks.label: Pairing 7 dots
blocks.description: Seven dots arranged as pairs ●● ●● ●● ● — three complete pairs and one unpaired dot, so 7 is odd.

blocks.text: A number is even when it can be written as 2 × n for some whole number n, and odd when it can be written as 2 × n + 1.
You do not need to pair huge numbers one by one. The **last digit** alone decides parity: if it is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 the number is even; if it is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 the number is odd.

content.text: The last digit works because every place except the units place contributes an even amount — tens are groups of 10, hundreds are groups of 100, and so on.

blocks.caption: Classifying numbers by their last digit

blocks.question: What is the parity of 63,547?

options.text: Odd, because the last digit 7 is odd
It cannot be decided without dividing by 2

blocks.explanation: The last digit 7 is odd, so 63,547 is odd. Digit sums decide divisibility by 3 or 9, not parity.

units.title: Parity of sums and differences
units.description: Predict whether a sum or difference is even or odd without doing the calculation.
learningObjectives: State the parity rules for adding and subtracting even and odd numbers

blocks.text: When two numbers are added or subtracted, their parities follow fixed patterns. You can read the parity of the answer without computing it.

The pattern is easy to see with pairing. Two odd numbers each have one unpaired dot; the two leftovers pair with **each other**, so an odd + odd is even. An even number has no leftover, so even + odd still has one leftover — it stays odd.
Same parity adds or subtracts to an even number; different parity adds or subtracts to an odd number.

content.text: 348 ends in 8 (even). 1,257 ends in 7 (odd). Even + odd is **odd**, so the answer must be odd — no addition needed.

blocks.title: Sums of many numbers
blocks.text: For a long sum, count the odd numbers. If the count of odd numbers is even, the total is even; if it is odd, the total is odd. Even numbers never change the parity of a sum.

blocks.question: Without computing: is 1,111 + 2,222 + 3,333 even or odd?

options.text: Even, because all numbers are even
Odd, because all three numbers are odd, and odd + odd + odd is odd
Even, because three odds always make an even
It depends on the order of addition

blocks.explanation: All three numbers are odd. odd + odd is even, and even + odd is odd — so three odds give an odd total.

units.title: Plus-minus signs
units.description: Use parity to settle the classic puzzle of placing + or − signs between 1 and 9.
learningObjectives: Show that the parity of a signed sum never changes
Apply the argument to the 1-to-9 sign puzzle

blocks.text: Here is a famous puzzle from the chapter: place a **+** or **−** sign in each gap of the expression below. Can any arrangement give an even answer?
Try a few arrangements first — every answer turns out odd. Parity explains why, instantly.

blocks.title: Worked example: why the answer is always odd

content.text: Start with all plus signs. The total is the sum of 1 to 9:
45 is odd. Now flip any single sign from + to −. The total drops by **twice** that number:
Subtracting an even number never changes parity. So every arrangement gives an odd total — an even answer is impossible.

blocks.text: Changing + k to − k changes a total by 2k, an even amount. So sign changes never alter the parity of the result.

blocks.title: Try it yourself
blocks.text: What about the numbers 1 to 8? Their sum is 36, which is even — so arrangements with an even answer (for example, 1 − 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 − 6 + 7 − 8 = 4) do exist. The starting parity decides everything.

blocks.question: In the puzzle 1 □ 2 □ … □ 10, which answers are possible?

options.text: Only odd answers, because the all-plus total 55 is odd
Neither — no arrangement gives a whole number

blocks.explanation: The all-plus total is 55, which is odd. Each sign flip subtracts an even number, so every result stays odd.

units.title: Parity in games and puzzles
units.description: Win number games and crack puzzles by tracking parity of products and sums.
learningObjectives: Decide the parity of products instantly
Use parity to predict winners in simple number games

blocks.text: Products follow an even stricter rule than sums: **if any factor is even, the product is even**. Only a product of all odd factors is odd.

content.text: Scan the factors: 27 is odd, 34 is even, 51 is odd. One even factor is enough.

blocks.text: Sums: parity depends on how many odd terms there are. Products: one even factor makes the whole product even.
Two players take turns choosing a number from 1 to 9, without repeats. The first player whose running total lands on an **even** number wins. Does the first player have a winning strategy?

Parity answers it: the first player picks an odd number, making the total odd. Whatever even the second player adds, the total stays odd. If the second player adds an odd number, the total becomes even — and the **second** player wins. So the first player should always respond to keep control: pick numbers so that after your move the total stays the parity you want.

blocks.question: Is the product 1 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 9 × 2 even or odd?

options.text: Odd, because most factors are odd
Even, because the factor 2 is even
Odd, because all factors are less than 10
It depends on the order of multiplication

blocks.explanation: A single even factor (2) makes the entire product even. Order of multiplication never affects parity.
